patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

cases.title: Welcome to Video — darknet CSAM site run from South Korea
cases.who: Welcome to Video (operator Son Jong-woo / Son Jung-woo)
cases.what: A Korean-run darknet site that sold access to child sexual abuse videos for Bitcoin; it held over 250,000 unique videos and its server had more than one million Bitcoin addresses, one per account. IRS-CI tracing of Bitcoin transactions located the server in South Korea, and the operator, Son Jong-woo, was arrested on 5 March 2018. On 16 October 2019 the US DOJ announced 337 users arrested and charged, with leads sent to 38 countries (Korean police counted 310 arrests in 32 countries, 223 of them Koreans). He served 18 months in South Korea; on 6 July 2020 the Seoul High Court refused US extradition, and in July 2022 he received a further 24 months for concealing proceeds. DOJ said 45% of the videos analysed had not been known before.
cases.cover_up: South Korean courts gave the operator 18 months on appeal (May 2019); Seoul High Court refused US extradition on 6 July 2020.

cases.title: Yemen — UN Group of Eminent Experts: rape of boys and girls by armed forces; sexual violence against recruited girls
cases.who: Security Belt Forces; Yemeni 35th Armoured Brigade; UAE personnel at Al-Bureiqa; Houthi de facto authorities
cases.what: The Group of Eminent Experts on Yemen, mandated by the UN Human Rights Council, reported in September 2019 (A/HRC/42/17) that Security Belt Forces raped 18 women, four boys and a girl in 2016–2019 and committed widespread rape of migrant women, girls and boys at a former facility in Aden; members of the 35th Armoured Brigade raped two boys; UAE personnel at Al-Bureiqa raped a boy; and Houthi detention sites saw sexual violence against a 17-year-old boy. Its September 2020 report found credible accounts that the Houthis recruited 34 girls aged 13–17 between June 2015 and June 2020, 12 of whom reportedly suffered sexual violence, forced early marriage linked to recruitment, or both. The Group said its figures were a small sample.

cases.title: Operation Atlas — Virtual Global Taskforce P2P sweep
cases.who: Peer-to-peer distributors and producers
cases.what: Ten Virtual Global Taskforce members (Australia, Colombia, Netherlands, Switzerland, US HSI, Korea, New Zealand, Canada, UAE, UK) arrested 303 people suspected of distributing and producing abuse material and identified 106 victims, announced November 2015.

cases.title: France charges Telegram founder Pavel Durov
cases.who: Telegram (messaging platform)
cases.what: Durov was arrested at Le Bourget airport on 24 August 2024 and on 28 August a Paris investigating judge placed him under formal investigation on all the charges for which he was arrested, including suspected complicity in running a platform allowing illicit transactions, images of child sexual abuse, drug trafficking and fraud, and refusal to communicate information to authorities. He was released on 5 million euros bail, required to report to police twice a week and barred from leaving France. A BBC investigation that month found Telegram was not a member of NCMEC or the IWF and had ignored repeated requests to join. On 4 December 2024 the IWF announced Telegram would use its hashes of known abuse images to detect such material in public parts of the platform; the IWF said it had confirmed thousands of reports of abuse imagery on Telegram since 2022.

networks.name: Welcome to Video
networks.what: Darknet video site paid in Bitcoin, about 1.2 million members; seized 2018. 337 arrests in 38 countries announced October 2019. Start year 2015 is not in the sources opened and is omitted from cases.

networks.name: Telegram
networks.what: Messaging platform; founder charged in France in August 2024 incl. complicity in distribution of CSAM; joined IWF in December 2024. Legal domicile Tortola (BVI), operational centre Dubai (Wikipedia).

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role: 1 case
patterns.role_note: Bangladesh — girls trafficked to India, Pakistan and the Gulf; Rohingya girls near Cox's Bazar (US TIP 2025).
patterns.pattern_summary: In 275 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

cases.title: Netherlands — Joustra committee: state failed to stop intercountry adoption abuses; all adoptions suspended
cases.who: Dutch government (Justice ministry), licensed Dutch adoption intermediaries, intermediaries in sending countries
cases.what: The Commission of Inquiry into Intercountry Adoption, set up in 2019 and chaired by Tjibbe Joustra, reported in February 2021 after a two-year investigation that found 'serious violations' in adoptions from countries including Sri Lanka, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Brazil and Colombia between 1967 and 1997/98, and concluded the Dutch government had for decades failed to prevent abuses and protect children's rights. The government suspended all intercountry adoptions with immediate effect on 8 February 2021. About 4,000 of the children were from Sri Lanka.
cases.cover_up: The government revealed in February 2021 that its officials were aware of wrongdoing for years and had failed to intervene (BBC).

cases.title: Myanmar — Tatmadaw sexual violence against Rohingya and ethnic minority women, girls and boys (UN FFM)
cases.who: Myanmar armed forces (Tatmadaw)
cases.what: The Independent International Fact-Finding Mission on Myanmar found in 2018 that hundreds of Rohingya women and girls were raped during the 2017 'clearance operations', 80% of corroborated cases being gang rapes, and its August 2019 report found sexual and gender-based violence a 'hallmark' of Tatmadaw operations in Rakhine, Kachin and Shan. It documented Rohingya men and boys, some as young as twelve, detained at Buthidaung prison in 2012 and subjected to sexual violence.

cases.title: Norway — NOU 2026:7 finds illegal and unethical intercountry adoptions
cases.who: Norwegian adoption organisations; Norwegian authorities; partner orphanages and bodies in 12 countries
cases.what: A government committee appointed in 2023 presented NOU 2026:7 'Forsvarlighet, risiko og tillit' on 22 June 2026. Examining adoptions from 12 countries since the 1950s, it concluded there were illegal or unethical conditions and that the Norwegian adoption system had clear shortcomings throughout the period. Individual findings included a kidnapped child adopted to Norway, a mother told she would get money if she consented, and documents deliberately falsified; payments to orphanages or organisations were sometimes linked to the number of children adopted.
cases.cover_up: Organisations did not always tell Norwegian authorities about payments or errors; authorities kept approving adoptions after learning of risks and illegalities.

cases.title: Kolkata red-light areas — rescues of trafficked Nepali girls and minors (2015, 2025)
cases.who: Brothel keepers and traffickers in Kolkata
cases.what: In January 2015 police, with International Justice Mission and three NGOs, freed six young women trafficked from Nepal from four brothels in Kolkata's largest red-light area; all had fake adult ID documents, which IJM said traffickers issue to underage girls. On 10 September 2025 Kolkata Police's Anti-Human Trafficking Unit rescued ten people including nine minor girls from a house in Burtolla, North Kolkata, and arrested six people, including the couple running it (charged). The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers recruit significant numbers of Nepali and Bangladeshi women and girls for sex trafficking in India.

cases.title: Bangladesh — girls trafficked to India, Pakistan and the Gulf; Rohingya girls near Cox's Bazar (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Traffickers, recruitment agents, armed groups in Rohingya camps
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers exploit Bangladeshi women and girls in sex trafficking abroad, including in India, Pakistan and Gulf countries, and observers estimate children are 40 per cent of Bangladeshi sex-trafficking victims exploited abroad. Tourists have increased demand for sexual exploitation, including of Rohingya girls, near Cox's Bazar, where more than one million Rohingya refugees live in 33 camps. Courts convicted 103 traffickers, down from 407.
cases.cover_up: Corruption and official complicity were significant concerns; corrupt policing in Rohingya camps.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role: First inquiry 2015 on
patterns.role_note: 2015: External Independent Review Panel on the UN response to sexual abuse by foreign forces in CAR (Deschamps, 2015).
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. In Italy the only national figures come from reports the Italian bishops' conference has published about itself since 2022. Brazil's Congress held inquiries into the sexual exploitation of children that reported in 2004, 2010 and 2014. The research for this map found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in the Philippines or India; India's official findings are state-level audits of children's homes, such as the 2018 audit of 110 homes in Bihar.

patterns.pattern: States that shielded their own
patterns.role: Where the children were
patterns.role_note: Burundian and Gabonese peacekeepers in the Central African Republic: Not charged (per Wikipedia citing UN/AP)
patterns.pattern_summary: When a person accused of abusing a child is a soldier, a diplomat or a foreign citizen, whether they are tried depends on their own government. UN peacekeepers can be prosecuted only by the country that sent them. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that at least 134 Sri Lankan peacekeepers had sexually exploited and abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007; 114 were sent home, and none was jailed in Sri Lanka. In 2013 the Vatican recalled its ambassador to the Dominican Republic, Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, while Dominican authorities were investigating him for abusing children, and later told Polish prosecutors that Vatican law did not allow him to be extradited. In 2020 a court in Seoul refused a US request to extradite Son Jong-woo, who had run the abuse website Welcome to Video. In 2013 Morocco's king pardoned Daniel Galván, a Spanish man convicted of raping children, as a gesture towards Spain. In Israel, a deputy health minister interfered with psychiatric assessments of Malka Leifer, which delayed her extradition to Australia for several years.

patterns.pattern: Peacekeepers and aid workers in crisis zones
patterns.role: Mission or crisis zone where children were abused
patterns.role_note: French Operation Sangaris soldiers — alleged abuse of children, Bangui. MINUSCA Burundian and Gabonese contingents — Dékoa allegations. MINUSCA peacekeepers — rapes near Bambari airport. MINUSCA — DR Congo battalion repatriated after child abuse allegations. MINUSCA — all Gabonese units withdrawn after SEA allegations (2021).
patterns.pattern_summary: In war zones and refugee camps, children have been sexually abused by soldiers and aid workers sent to protect them or to provide food and shelter. In 2002 a report by the UN refugee agency and Save the Children described aid workers and peacekeepers in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone trading food and other aid for sex with children. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that Sri Lankan peacekeepers had abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007, and 114 soldiers were sent home; none was jailed in Sri Lanka. An independent commission found 83 alleged perpetrators among people working on the World Health Organization's Ebola response in the Democratic Republic of the Congo between 2018 and 2020, 21 of them WHO staff, and victims as young as 13. The UN has published yearly counts of these allegations against peacekeepers since 2004.

patterns.pattern: War and the taking of children
patterns.role: Abductions and sexual violence by armed groups
patterns.role_note: Central African Republic — UN-verified sexual violence and abduction of children (2024).
patterns.pattern_summary: Armed groups have abducted, enslaved and sold children as a deliberate practice. In 2014 the group calling itself Islamic State captured Yazidi women and children in northern Iraq and sold girls as sexual slaves; a UN commission reported in 2016 that more than 3,200 women and children were still held. In 2014 Boko Haram abducted 276 schoolgirls from Chibok in north-eastern Nigeria, and 82 were still captive in 2024. The Lord's Resistance Army abducted children in Uganda and the neighbouring countries over many years; in 2021 the International Criminal Court convicted one of its commanders, Dominic Ongwen, on 61 counts, including forced marriage and sexual slavery. UN fact-finding missions found sexual violence against children by Myanmar's army and by Sudan's Rapid Support Forces, against girls as young as eight. The UN verifies and publishes these attacks country by country each year.

cases.title: Lord's Resistance Army — child abduction and sexual slavery; ICC conviction of Dominic Ongwen
cases.who: Lord's Resistance Army (LRA), leader Joseph Kony (ICC warrant outstanding)
cases.what: The LRA abducted tens of thousands of children in northern Uganda for use as fighters, porters and 'wives'; UNICEF estimated at least 25,000 by 2006. On 4 February 2021 ICC Trial Chamber IX convicted Sinia Brigade commander Dominic Ongwen, himself abducted as a child, of 61 crimes including rape, sexual slavery, forced marriage, forced pregnancy and the conscription and use of children under 15 (2002–2005); he was sentenced to 25 years on 6 May 2021, confirmed on appeal 15 December 2022. From 2008 the LRA abducted thousands more in DR Congo, South Sudan and CAR.

cases.title: MINUSCA Burundian and Gabonese contingents — Dékoa allegations
cases.who: UN Multidimensional Integrated Stabilization Mission in CAR (MINUSCA) military contingents from Burundi and Gabon
cases.what: The Secretary-General's 2017 report states that two allegations recorded in MINUSCA, concerning incidents in Dékoa and military personnel from Gabon and Burundi, led to interviews of some 136 alleged victims and accounted for 48% of all victims recorded in 2016. Investigations by the troop-contributing countries were still pending. Press accounts reported that at least 98 girls described abuse and 41 troops were identified and sent home without charges.

cases.title: Central African Republic — UN-verified sexual violence and abduction of children (2024)
cases.who: CPC coalition (UPC, 3R, anti-balaka); national defence forces; Wagner Ti Azande/Azande Ani Kpi Gbe; RSF
cases.what: The UN verified sexual violence against 114 girls in CAR in 2024: CPC armed groups 58, government and pro-government forces 35 (national defence forces 21, Wagner Ti Azande/Azande Ani Kpi Gbe 9), PRNC 11, Sudanese RSF 2. It verified the abduction of 141 children, most for recruitment and/or sexual violence. The Secretary-General said he was deeply concerned by rising violations by government and pro-government forces.

cases.title: UN — Secretary-General's annual SEA reports: 27 child victims in peacekeeping and political missions in 2024
cases.who: UN peacekeepers, civilian staff, agency staff and implementing partners
cases.what: The Secretary-General reports each year to the General Assembly on special measures for protection from sexual exploitation and abuse. The report released in March 2025 recorded 102 allegations in peacekeeping and political missions in 2024, 44 in DR Congo and 40 in the Central African Republic, with 125 victims, 27 of them children; there were also 190 allegations against staff of UN agencies, funds and programmes and 382 against staff of implementing partners. The supplementary tables list child victims in MINUSCA (Central African Republic, 13), MONUSCO (DR Congo, 9), UNMISS (South Sudan, 2), UNMIL (Liberia, 2) and UNITAD (Iraq, 1). It noted about 750 paternity claims involving peacekeepers since 2006, more than 500 still pending.
cases.cover_up: About 750 paternity and child support claims against peacekeeping personnel since 2006, more than 500 still pending; claims are referred to troop-contributing countries, most of which have not taken meaningful action

cases.title: Central African Republic — Deschamps panel finds 'gross institutional failure' by the UN over child abuse by foreign troops (2015)
cases.who: French Sangaris forces; Chadian and Equatorial Guinean MISCA soldiers; UN officials who handled the allegations
cases.what: The External Independent Review Panel appointed by the Secretary-General and chaired by Marie Deschamps reported on 17 December 2015. It examined accounts by boys aged about 8 to 13 sheltering at the M'Poko camp in Bangui that soldiers, largely from the French Sangaris force, and also Chadian and Equatorial Guinean MISCA troops, had sexually abused them between December 2013 and June 2014, often in exchange for food or money. It called the UN's handling a 'gross institutional failure' and found that three senior UN officials had abused their authority.
cases.cover_up: Report passed 'from inbox to inbox'; panel found abuse of authority by the head of MINUSCA's Human Rights and Justice Section, the SRSG for MINUSCA and the head of OIOS, and that staff became more concerned with whether the allegations had been improperly leaked to French authorities than with acting on them

cases.title: MINUSCA — all Gabonese units withdrawn after SEA allegations (2021)
cases.who: Gabonese military contingent, MINUSCA
cases.what: On 15 September 2021 the UN announced that all Gabonese military units in MINUSCA (about 450 personnel) would be repatriated after allegations of sexual exploitation and abuse; Gabon opened an investigation. The Secretary-General's 2022 report links most multiple-victim MINUSCA allegations of 2021 to one troop-contributing country repatriated that September.

cases.title: MINUSCA peacekeepers — rapes near Bambari airport
cases.who: MINUSCA contingents believed by survivors to be from the Republic of Congo or DR Congo
cases.what: Human Rights Watch documented eight cases of sexual exploitation and abuse by MINUSCA peacekeepers during research in Bambari in January 2016, including a 14-year-old girl and an 18-year-old woman who said they were gang-raped near Bambari airport. Most incidents occurred between September and December 2015, when a Republic of Congo contingent guarded the airport.

cases.title: MINUSCA — DR Congo battalion repatriated after child abuse allegations
cases.who: Armed Forces of the DRC (FARDC) battalion serving with MINUSCA
cases.what: About 800 troops from the Democratic Republic of the Congo served with the UN mission in the Central African Republic (MINUSCA) in 2015. In August 2015 three Congolese peacekeepers were accused of raping three female civilians, including a minor. In January 2016 MINUSCA confirmed the Congolese unit would withdraw and not be replaced, after a UN review of its equipment, vetting procedures and preparedness; it was not clear whether the abuse allegations were the main factor. The UN's 2016 allegations tables (A/71/818) list 17 allegations involving DRC military personnel in MINUSCA, with 15 child victims.

cases.title: French Operation Sangaris soldiers — alleged abuse of children, Bangui
cases.who: French army, Operation Sangaris (not under UN command)
cases.what: An internal UN document revealed by The Guardian in April 2015 recorded interviews with six boys aged 9 to 13 who said French soldiers of Operation Sangaris had sexually abused them between December 2013 and June 2014 at the displaced persons' camp at Bangui's M'Poko airport, in exchange for food rations. The Paris prosecutor had opened a preliminary inquiry in July 2014; the investigation eventually covered accusations by fifteen children, most interviewed in Bangui in 2015 and 2016. In January 2018 French investigating judges dismissed the case (non-lieu) for lack of sufficient charges, citing inconsistencies in testimony; the prosecutor said 'it cannot be affirmed at the end of the investigation that no sexual abuse was committed'. No soldier was charged.
cases.cover_up: The internal UN report was not passed to French authorities by the UN; the UN official who passed it on (Anders Kompass) was suspended and resigned in 2016 in protest at impunity.

patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role: Sent abusers to another country
patterns.role_note: Dominican Republic → Vatican: Nuncio Józef Wesołowski; Dominican Republic → Poland: Fr Wojciech Gil.
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, religious brother, teacher or head teacher was found to be abusing children, the institution they worked for often moved them instead of reporting them to the police. The move was to another parish, another school, another state or another country, and the person went on working with children. A Pennsylvania grand jury reported in 2018 that bishops in six dioceses had moved priests they knew to be abusers. In Australia, Bishop Mulkearns knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children and kept appointing him to new parishes. In Melbourne in 2008, the Adass Israel School paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. In England, an internal report in 1982 described how the barrister John Smyth had beaten boys he met through evangelical holiday camps; he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, the police were not told until 2013, and a 2024 review called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa". The map draws 34 documented moves and colors the countries that sent or received an abuser.

patterns.role: Where the children were
patterns.role_note: Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, nuncio to the Dominican Republic: Laicised 2014; Vatican trial on child-pornography charges announced June 2015; died 27 August 2015 before trial
patterns.pattern_summary: When a person accused of abusing a child is a soldier, a diplomat or a foreign citizen, whether they are tried depends on their own government. UN peacekeepers can be prosecuted only by the country that sent them. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that at least 134 Sri Lankan peacekeepers had sexually exploited and abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007; 114 were sent home, and none was jailed in Sri Lanka. In 2013 the Vatican recalled its ambassador to the Dominican Republic, Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, while Dominican authorities were investigating him for abusing children, and later told Polish prosecutors that Vatican law did not allow him to be extradited. In 2020 a court in Seoul refused a US request to extradite Son Jong-woo, who had run the abuse website Welcome to Video. In 2013 Morocco's king pardoned Daniel Galván, a Spanish man convicted of raping children, as a gesture towards Spain. In Israel, a deputy health minister interfered with psychiatric assessments of Malka Leifer, which delayed her extradition to Australia for several years.

cases.title: Sosúa — 29 trafficking victims including 20 minors freed in US–Dominican sting (2015)
cases.who: Local pimping ring in a tourist town
cases.what: In April 2015 Dominican authorities, with HSI Santo Domingo and two private US organisations, lured alleged traffickers to a staged 'sex party' in the tourist town of Sosúa, freeing 29 victims including 20 minors aged 14–17 and arresting seven Dominican nationals (two women, five men), who faced up to 15 years. The 2025 US TIP report says teenage girls are frequently exploited on streets, in parks and on beaches, and NGOs link rising child victim numbers to weak regulation of tourism.

cases.title: Nuncio Józef Wesołowski and Fr Wojciech Gil — Dominican Republic
cases.who: Apostolic Nunciature in the Dominican Republic; Archbishop Józef Wesołowski; Fr Wojciech Gil
cases.what: Polish Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, papal nuncio to the Dominican Republic from 2008, was recalled in 2013 amid allegations of abusing minors, and Dominican prosecutors opened a criminal investigation on 4 September 2013. A church tribunal found him guilty and the Vatican announced his laicisation on 27 June 2014. In June 2015 a Vatican prosecutor indicted him for abusing children in the Dominican Republic in 2008–2013 and for possessing child abuse images, but he was found dead in his Vatican rooms in August 2015, before trial. Fr Wojciech Gil, a Polish priest who had worked in the Dominican Republic, was arrested in Poland in February 2014; on 25 March 2015 a court in Wołomin sentenced him to seven years for abusing six minors in the Dominican Republic (2009–2013) and two in Poland.
cases.cover_up: Wesołowski recalled to the Vatican in August 2013 before Dominican authorities opened an investigation; Gil returned to Poland, which has no extradition treaty with the Dominican Republic

patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role: Received abusers from another country
patterns.role_note: Australia → Fiji: Salesian Julian Fox; Australia / New Zealand → Fiji: transferred clergy.
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, religious brother, teacher or head teacher was found to be abusing children, the institution they worked for often moved them instead of reporting them to the police. The move was to another parish, another school, another state or another country, and the person went on working with children. A Pennsylvania grand jury reported in 2018 that bishops in six dioceses had moved priests they knew to be abusers. In Australia, Bishop Mulkearns knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children and kept appointing him to new parishes. In Melbourne in 2008, the Adass Israel School paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. In England, an internal report in 1982 described how the barrister John Smyth had beaten boys he met through evangelical holiday camps; he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, the police were not told until 2013, and a 2024 review called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa". The map draws 34 documented moves and colors the countries that sent or received an abuser.

In July 2020 1News reported that some of about 1,300 alleged child abuse cases involving clergy in Fiji concerned clergy from Australia and New Zealand.
cases.cover_up: Fox was transferred to Fiji in 1999 after Australian police began investigating; the Fiji church knew of allegations nine years before he was charged

patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role: No survey data on online abuse in its region
patterns.role_note: Childlight's 2026 update found West and Central Africa lacking representative survey data on technology-facilitated child sexual exploitation.
patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

cases.title: Croatia — first priest convictions
cases.who: Catholic dioceses in Croatia
cases.what: In 2000 Fr Ivan Čuček was convicted of abusing 37 girls; his three-year sentence was cut to 18 months by the Supreme Court. In 2007 Fr Drago Ljubičić of Rab became the first Croatian priest to serve prison time, three years for molesting five teenage boys. Fr Nediljko Ivanov of Bibinje became the first priest convicted by a Croatian church court, but civil prosecution was time-barred.
cases.cover_up: Nediljko Ivanov, whose abuse 1983–1991 was reported in 2012, was time-barred; a church court ordered only prayer, fasting and an apology and he continued to say Mass

cases.title: New Zealand DIA-led operation: 146 children safeguarded
cases.who: Tens of thousands of accounts sharing abuse material on an online service
cases.what: Begun in 2019 after an online service provider reported offenders exchanging imagery of the sadistic abuse of infants and children. By March 2022 it had opened 836 cases internationally, led to 46 arrests across New Zealand, identified more than 100 suspects in the EU and safeguarded 146 children; in Austria and Hungary suspects were abusing their own children.

patterns.role: First inquiry 2005–2014

patterns.pattern: Platforms, servers and the money behind them
patterns.role: Hosts the most reported abuse material (IWF 2025)
patterns.role_note: 7,455 web addresses actioned by the IWF in 2025 (2% of the total).
patterns.pattern_summary: Online abuse of children depends on ordinary businesses: companies that host websites, apps and social platforms, payment services and banks. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes abuse images, found most of the material it removed on servers in Bulgaria, the United States, the Netherlands, Romania and France. Reports of suspected abuse to the US CyberTipline, most of them made by American technology companies, rose from 4,560 in 1998 to more than 36 million in 2023, then fell to about 20.5 million in 2024; the centre that runs it attributed part of the fall to Meta encrypting its messages. Money for watching abuse streamed live flows from Australia, Britain, the United States and other wealthy countries to the Philippines. In 2020 the Australian bank Westpac agreed to pay a A$1.3 billion penalty for breaches of money-laundering law that included failing to check payments that could be linked to child exploitation. The classified advertising site Backpage earned more than $500 million from advertisements, including ones used to sell children, before US authorities shut it down in 2018.

cases.title: Iceland — Catholic Church investigative commission on Landakotsskóli (2012)
cases.who: Catholic Church in Iceland; Landakotsskóli school and church summer camps
cases.what: An investigative commission of the Catholic Church in Iceland, chaired by Hjördís Hákonardóttir, reported in early November 2012. It confirmed that Rev. Ágúst Georg, principal of the church's Landakotsskóli school, and teacher Margrét Müller abused pupils. Of 30 former pupils and summer-camp children questioned, 8 said they had been sexually abused and 27 described mental abuse. It found that Bishop Joannes Gijsen destroyed a letter reporting abuse by the priest. In December 2015 the Althing passed Act No. 117/2015, extending the state compensation scheme for abuse in institutions to Landakotsskóli.
cases.cover_up: The commission reported that Bishop Joannes Gijsen destroyed a letter from a man who said the priest had abused him.

cases.title: Dreamboard / Operation Delego
cases.who: Dreamboard (invitation-only bulletin board, about 600 members)
cases.what: An invitation-only bulletin board, used by an estimated 600 people, whose applicants had to upload abuse material of children aged 12 or under and keep uploading to stay. NBC reported the computers hosting the site were in Georgia, US, and the top administrators were in France and Canada. In August 2011 Attorney General Eric Holder and DHS Secretary Janet Napolitano announced charges against 72 people, with arrests on five continents including 43 in the US. By January 2013, 57 had been arrested, 45 had pleaded guilty and one was convicted at trial; 42 had been sentenced to between 10 years and life. Fifteen were known only by online identities. DOJ said at least 38 children were being abused by group members.

cases.title: 'Hidden in Plain Sight' — Australian Parliament recognises orphanage trafficking as modern slavery
cases.who: Australian volunteers, donors, schools and tour operators supporting overseas orphanages
cases.what: The Joint Standing Committee's report 'Hidden in Plain Sight', released on 6 December 2017 from its inquiry into establishing a Modern Slavery Act, recognised orphanage trafficking as a form of modern slavery to be covered by the Act. A chapter was devoted to orphanage trafficking, orphanage tourism and Australian donations, with evidence from ReThink Orphanages, Lumos, the ChildSafe campaign and others. Australia's Modern Slavery Act followed in 2018; Lumos supported the change.

cases.title: SOS Children's Villages — Independent Special Commission (ISC) worldwide report (2023)
cases.who: SOS Children's Villages (federation of member associations; International Senate); former senior staff
cases.what: An Independent Special Commission appointed by the International Senate of SOS Children's Villages in 2021, chaired by former Kenyan Chief Justice Willy Mutunga with former Delhi High Court acting chief justice Gita Mittal, issued its summary report on 6 June 2023. Using a 'reasonable grounds to believe' standard, it confirmed serious allegations of child sexual and physical abuse in several member associations in Africa, Asia and Central America, and found cover-ups of past sexual abuse and failures to report to national authorities in more than one association. Countries named in the report include Nepal, Cambodia, India, Kenya, Panama, Sierra Leone and Syria. A confidential 991-page part two went to the organisation's Senate and Executive Board on 2 May 2023; in November 2025 SOS Children's Villages International said it was examining whether parts could be passed to prosecutors.
cases.cover_up: Former senior staff in some member associations knew of abuse and failed to act or concealed reports; serious abuse was not reported to national authorities.

cases.title: Kenya coast — UNICEF/Government study on child sex tourism (2006)
cases.who: Tourists and local clients in Kenya's beach resorts
cases.what: On 19 December 2006 UNICEF and Kenya's Ministry of Home Affairs launched a joint study of four beach resort areas. It found that up to 30 per cent of 12–18-year-old girls living there were involved in casual sex work and that two to three thousand children were in full-time commercial sex; 38 per cent of clients were Kenyan and 44 per cent Italian, German or Swiss tourists. Vice President Moody Awori accepted the findings and acknowledged police and community failure to enforce the law.

cases.title: Kenya — child sex trafficking in Kilifi/Kwale villas; Karamoja girls to Nairobi (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Family members, taxi drivers, recruiters; foreign and local offenders
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report cites a 2023 NGO study estimating that more than 2,000 children were exploited in child sex trafficking in Kilifi and Kwale counties, increasingly in private villas and vacation homes rather than hotels. It also reports cross-border rings moving women and underage girls from Uganda's Karamoja region to Nairobi, and truck drivers, miners and Lake Victoria fishermen exploiting children.
cases.cover_up: The report notes ongoing concerns of official complicity with no reported action against complicit officials.

cases.title: Kenya — babies stolen and sold in Nairobi, incl. from a government hospital (BBC Africa Eye)
cases.who: Street child-snatchers working for a buyer; illegal street clinics; a clinical social worker at a government hospital
cases.what: A year-long BBC Africa Eye investigation (November 2020) found children snatched from homeless mothers in Nairobi and sold for about £350–550, illegal street clinics selling newborns (one offered an unborn child for about £315 while paying the mother £70), and a clinical social worker at the government-run Mama Lucy Kibaki Hospital who sold an abandoned two-week-old boy to undercover reporters for 300,000 shillings (£2,000) using legitimate transfer paperwork. The reporters delivered all the children to a children's home. The BBC said the official appeared to keep his job and the clinic appeared to still operate.

flows.title: Karamoja, Uganda → Nairobi (girls for domestic servitude and sex)
flows.what: Cross-border rings ferry women and underage girls from Karamoja to Nairobi for domestic servitude or sex trafficking.

flows.title: Italy / Germany / Switzerland → Kenya coast (tourist offenders)
flows.what: The 2006 UNICEF–Government study found Italian, German and Swiss tourists made up 44 per cent of clients of exploited children on the coast; Kenyans were 38 per cent.

flows.title: United Kingdom → Kenya (Keith Morris)
flows.what: Keith Morris was jailed for 18.5 years in the UK for 10 sexual offences against vulnerable children in Kenya, one of about eight UK prosecutions for offences abroad since 1997.

patterns.role: Sending country, later closed or suspended

Sri Lanka, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Brazil, Colombia
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.role: Home country of accused troops or staff

patterns.pattern_summary: In war zones and refugee camps, children have been sexually abused by soldiers and aid workers sent to protect them or to provide food and shelter. In 2002 a report by the UN refugee agency and Save the Children described aid workers and peacekeepers in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone trading food and other aid for sex with children. In the Central African Republic, children reported abuse by French soldiers and UN troops in 2014 and 2015; French judges closed the case against the French soldiers in 2018 without charges. An independent commission found 83 alleged perpetrators among people working on the World Health Organization's Ebola response in the Democratic Republic of the Congo between 2018 and 2020, 21 of them WHO staff, and victims as young as 13. The UN has published yearly counts of these allegations against peacekeepers since 2004.

cases.title: MINUSTAH Sri Lankan contingent — child sexual exploitation ring, Haiti
cases.who: Sri Lanka Army contingent of the UN Stabilization Mission in Haiti (MINUSTAH)
cases.what: In November 2007, 114 members of the 950-strong Sri Lankan contingent were accused of sexual misconduct and abuse, and 108, including three officers, were sent home. The UN Office of Internal Oversight Services concluded that 'acts of sexual exploitation and abuse (against children) were frequent and occurred usually at night, and at virtually every location where the contingent personnel were deployed', and said charges should include statutory rape. An Associated Press investigation in April 2017 found that at least 134 Sri Lankan peacekeepers had exploited at least nine children in a sex ring between 2004 and 2007; none was jailed.
cases.cover_up: Repatriation instead of prosecution: 114 Sri Lankan peacekeepers were sent home; Sri Lankan authorities judged the acts 'consensual' and nobody was jailed.

cases.title: Netherlands — Joustra committee: state failed to stop intercountry adoption abuses; all adoptions suspended
cases.who: Dutch government (Justice ministry), licensed Dutch adoption intermediaries, intermediaries in sending countries
cases.what: The Commission of Inquiry into Intercountry Adoption, set up in 2019 and chaired by Tjibbe Joustra, reported in February 2021 after a two-year investigation that found 'serious violations' in adoptions from countries including Sri Lanka, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Brazil and Colombia between 1967 and 1997/98, and concluded the Dutch government had for decades failed to prevent abuses and protect children's rights. The government suspended all intercountry adoptions with immediate effect on 8 February 2021. About 4,000 of the children were from Sri Lanka.
cases.cover_up: The government revealed in February 2021 that its officials were aware of wrongdoing for years and had failed to intervene (BBC).

cases.title: Sweden — state inquiry into intercountry adoptions (report 2 June 2025)
cases.who: Swedish state authorities and adoption organisations
cases.what: Sweden's independent inquiry into intercountry adoptions issued its report on 2 June 2025 (nearly 1,600 pages), reviewing 65 years of adoption history and documenting numerous irregularities and illegalities of which state authorities had some knowledge. Sweden had already stopped adoptions from South Korea (AP, 2024). Sweden received 9,051 Korean children 1957–2005, and in January 1975 the Swedish ambassador urged South Korea to continue sending children after it tried to halt adoptions to Scandinavia.

cases.title: Norway — NOU 2026:7 finds illegal and unethical intercountry adoptions
cases.who: Norwegian adoption organisations; Norwegian authorities; partner orphanages and bodies in 12 countries
cases.what: A government committee appointed in 2023 presented NOU 2026:7 'Forsvarlighet, risiko og tillit' on 22 June 2026. Examining adoptions from 12 countries since the 1950s, it concluded there were illegal or unethical conditions and that the Norwegian adoption system had clear shortcomings throughout the period. Individual findings included a kidnapped child adopted to Norway, a mother told she would get money if she consented, and documents deliberately falsified; payments to orphanages or organisations were sometimes linked to the number of children adopted.
cases.cover_up: Organisations did not always tell Norwegian authorities about payments or errors; authorities kept approving adoptions after learning of risks and illegalities.

cases.title: Sri Lanka — 1980s 'baby farms' supplying intercountry adoption
cases.who: Baby farms, brokers, hospital doctors and nurses acting as intermediaries for Western agencies
cases.what: A Dutch Zembla documentary (September 2017) reported that babies were bought or abducted from hospitals, handed to paid 'acting mothers' and sold for adoption, mainly to the Netherlands, with others to the UK, Sweden and Germany. Sri Lanka's health minister Rajitha Senaratne acknowledged on camera that 'there were a lot of baby farms back then' and announced an inquiry and a DNA databank. Sri Lanka changed its rules after a 1987 police raid found 20 newborns and 22 women held in 'prison like conditions'.
cases.cover_up: Adoption records were widely falsified; 'acting mothers' were paid to pose as birth mothers in court.

cases.title: Switzerland — authorities' irregularities in intercountry adoptions (Sri Lanka, India, Tibet…); proposed ban
cases.who: Swiss federal and cantonal authorities; private adoption agencies
cases.what: Swiss authorities soon realised that the placement of children for adoption, often wrongly presented as orphans, was also driven by economic interests and linked to organised child trafficking; decisions were often made on incomplete or falsified documents, and checks on foster families and on legal requirements were insufficient. From the 2010s, under pressure from groups such as Back to the Roots, intercountry adoptions from Tibet, Sri Lanka and India drew public attention. In 2018 the Federal Assembly commissioned a study on intercountry adoption; the Federal Council acknowledged the authorities' irregularities and omissions in 2020 and 2023, and at the end of 2024 recommended a general ban on intercountry adoption.

cases.title: Seth Sevana children's home, Vavuniya — monk arrested, bail with NCPA consent
cases.who: Seth Sevana Lama Nivasa children's home (run by a Buddhist monk) housing war-affected Tamil children; National Child Protection Authority (NCPA)
cases.what: In October 2013 the head of a children's home in Vavuniya, a Buddhist monk, was arrested for sexually abusing a 9-year-old child, confirmed by medical evidence on 12 October 2013. The NCPA took custody of the other 22 children on 15 October 2013. Most children were war-affected Tamil children placed by poor families. Groundviews reported that complaints had reached the NCPA since 2010 and that the agency later supported his release on bail.
cases.cover_up: Complaints had been made to the NCPA since 2010; the arrest came only after protests by Vavuniya child protection officers. On 31 December 2013 the monk got unconditional bail after the Attorney General's Department, on NCPA instructions, told the court it had no objection; the NCPA did not submit the 22 children's reports to the court.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role: First inquiry 2015 on
patterns.role_note: 2020: Marshall Islands — Paul Petersen adoption scheme, Arizona/Utah/Arkansas prosecutions.
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. In Italy the only national figures come from reports the Italian bishops' conference has published about itself since 2022. Brazil's Congress held inquiries into the sexual exploitation of children that reported in 2004, 2010 and 2014. The research for this map found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in the Philippines or India; India's official findings are state-level audits of children's homes, such as the 2018 audit of 110 homes in Bihar.

patterns.pattern_summary: In 275 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. cases.title: Marshall Islands — Paul Petersen 'baby mill' adoption scheme

patterns.role: Hosts the most reported abuse material (IWF 2025)
patterns.role_note: 17,046 web addresses actioned by the IWF in 2025 (5% of the total).
patterns.pattern_summary: Online abuse of children depends on ordinary businesses: companies that host websites, apps and social platforms, payment services and banks. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes abuse images, found most of the material it removed on servers in Bulgaria, the United States, the Netherlands, Romania and France. Reports of suspected abuse to the US CyberTipline, most of them made by American technology companies, rose from 4,560 in 1998 to more than 36 million in 2023, then fell to about 20.5 million in 2024; the centre that runs it attributed part of the fall to Meta encrypting its messages. In 2020 the Australian bank Westpac agreed to pay a A$1.3 billion penalty for breaches of money-laundering law that included failing to check payments that could be linked to child exploitation. The classified advertising site Backpage earned more than $500 million from advertisements, including ones used to sell children, before US authorities shut it down in 2018.

cases.title: Malaysia — government task force confirms rape of Penan schoolgirls by timber workers in Sarawak (2009)
cases.who: Workers of Malaysian logging companies in Sarawak (no company named)
cases.what: A team from Malaysia's Ministry of Women, Family and Community Development investigated in Sarawak in November 2008, and its report, made public in September 2009 after the Associated Press obtained it, found that timber workers had raped or tried to sexually abuse Penan schoolgirls, some as young as 10, including girls given lifts to school in logging trucks. Sarawak police said three complaints had been investigated the previous year without enough evidence to prosecute.

cases.title: Global Ikhwan (GISB) children's homes — Operation Global
cases.who: Global Ikhwan Services and Business Holdings (GISB), linked to the banned Al-Arqam movement
cases.what: On 11 September 2024 Malaysian police raided 20 charity homes linked to GISB Holdings in Selangor and Negeri Sembilan, rescued 402 children aged 1 to 17 and arrested 171 adults, after six months of intelligence work; police said they had received 41 reports about the group since 2011. By 10 October police put the total rescued at 625. Three madrasah student assistants in Kuala Pilah were charged with 14 counts of sexually abusing five children in 2022–2023, another teaching assistant with sexually assaulting four boys, and others with physical abuse of children; police said the investigation pointed to organised crime and human trafficking.

cases.title: Malaysia — online baby-selling trade (Al Jazeera 101 East)
cases.who: Online brokers; baby sellers
cases.what: An undercover Al Jazeera 101 East investigation (24 November 2016) documented an online trade in which babies were advertised with photos and sold for thousands of dollars, with buyers choosing by gender, race and skin colour. Some babies went to couples wanting a child; others, it reported, were sold to traffickers. Immigrant sex workers who cannot legally bear children in Malaysia were among those giving up babies.

cases.title: Welcome to Video — darknet CSAM site run from South Korea
cases.who: Welcome to Video (operator Son Jong-woo / Son Jung-woo)
cases.what: A Korean-run darknet site that sold access to child sexual abuse videos for Bitcoin; it held over 250,000 unique videos and its server had more than one million Bitcoin addresses, one per account. IRS-CI tracing of Bitcoin transactions located the server in South Korea, and the operator, Son Jong-woo, was arrested on 5 March 2018. On 16 October 2019 the US DOJ announced 337 users arrested and charged, with leads sent to 38 countries (Korean police counted 310 arrests in 32 countries, 223 of them Koreans). He served 18 months in South Korea; on 6 July 2020 the Seoul High Court refused US extradition, and in July 2022 he received a further 24 months for concealing proceeds. DOJ said 45% of the videos analysed had not been known before.
cases.cover_up: South Korean courts gave the operator 18 months on appeal (May 2019); Seoul High Court refused US extradition on 6 July 2020.

patterns.pattern: Children taken by governments, then abused or given false identities
patterns.role: Dictatorship or occupation: children given to other families under false identities
patterns.role_note: Nazi Germany — kidnapping of Polish and other children for Germanization (RuSHA trial) (receiving or involved).
patterns.pattern_summary: In several countries the government itself took children from their parents, and the records show those children were then sexually abused or handed to other families under false identities. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, babies born to women held in secret detention were taken and given to military families and allies of the regime. In 2012 a Buenos Aires court found this had been a "systematic plan" and sentenced the former dictator Jorge Videla to 50 years. By July 2025 the Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo had identified 140 of those children. Uruguay, Chile, El Salvador and Franco's Spain had similar cases, in which children were taken without their parents' consent and adopted by other families at home or abroad, often under changed names. Nazi Germany took children from occupied Poland and placed them with German families under new identities. In Canada and the United States, Indigenous children were sent to government-funded residential and boarding schools. Canada's Truth and Reconciliation Commission reported in 2015, and by the end of 2014 nearly 38,000 claims had been made for physical and sexual abuse at the schools. A US federal report in 2022 said many children at its 417 boarding schools suffered physical, sexual and emotional abuse. Britain sent children abroad to Australia, Canada and other countries under child migration schemes, and a 2018 inquiry found evidence that children sent under these schemes were sexually abused. In Ireland and South Korea, inquiries found that adoption agencies working with the state falsely registered children as orphans or hid their identities.

patterns.pattern_summary: In 275 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

cases.title: Project Spade — Azov Films, Toronto
cases.who: Azov Films (Toronto distributor of 'naturist' films of children)
cases.what: Toronto police undercover officers made contact with a man sharing graphic abuse images in October 2010, which led to Azov Films, a Toronto company run by Brian Way that produced and sold films of child exploitation worldwide; after a joint investigation with the US Postal Inspection Service, police raided the business. Police said it was a $4 million business distributing to over 50 countries and seized over 45 terabytes of data. On 14 November 2013 Toronto police announced 348 arrests and 386 children rescued; those arrested included 40 school teachers, nine doctors and nurses, six law enforcement personnel, nine pastors and priests and three foster parents. Way was arrested in 2011 and in 2016 was found guilty of making and distributing child sexual abuse material and sentenced to ten years, reduced after a judge found he had been abused in jail.
cases.cover_up: Germany's BKA received the customer list in October 2011 but began investigating only in October 2012; a German MP on the list later resigned, and information about the case was passed to his party leader.

cases.title: Nazi Germany — kidnapping of Polish and other children for Germanization (RuSHA trial)
cases.who: SS Race and Settlement Main Office (RuSHA), Lebensborn e.V., SS
cases.what: Nazi Germany seized children judged 'racially valuable' in occupied Poland and elsewhere, held them in Lebensborn and other homes and placed them with German families under new identities; DW reports estimates of up to 200,000 Polish children kidnapped and forcibly 'Germanized'. In the RuSHA trial (United States v. Ulrich Greifelt et al., Nuremberg Military Tribunal I), 14 leading officials of the SS Race and Settlement Main Office, Lebensborn and related bodies were charged with crimes including the kidnapping of 'racially valuable' children; charges were read on 10 October 1947, the trial ran from 20 October 1947 to 17 February 1948, and on 10 March 1948 the tribunal convicted 13 — Greifelt was sentenced to life — and acquitted one.

cases.title: Ukraine — rape and sexual violence by Russian forces incl. children (UN Commission of Inquiry)
cases.who: Russian armed forces and authorities
cases.what: The Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine found that Russian authorities committed the war crimes of rape and other sexual violence; cases it investigated included a 16-year-old girl, and in September 2022 it said it had documented children raped, tortured and unlawfully confined. Ukraine's official Children of War platform records 23 children sexually abused, according to the Office of the Prosecutor General.

cases.title: LS Models / 'Alex Model' raids, Ukraine
cases.who: 'Alex Model' agency (LS-Models brands)
cases.what: A Kyiv modelling agency with branches in Kharkiv and Simferopol recruited children through TV, newspaper and radio adverts and produced sexualised images sold worldwide under 'LS' brands from 2001. Police raided it in July 2004; at the same time over 150 people were arrested in Australia for possession and distribution.
cases.cover_up: Despite surveillance and arrests the legal outcome was described as lenient.

cases.title: Ukraine orphanages as a 'recruitment tool' for traffickers — Disability Rights International 'No Way Home'
cases.who: Ukrainian state orphanages, boarding schools and institutions for children with disabilities
cases.what: Disability Rights International investigated 33 institutions between 2012 and 2015 and published 'No Way Home' in 2015. La Strada Ukraine told DRI that recruiting children from orphanages into prostitution is 'the most typical scheme' and that sexual exploitation in institutions typically begins around age 13, often instigated by staff; an IOM counter-trafficking coordinator called orphanages a direct feeder to domestic and international trafficking and said most documented cases originate in the vocational schools that orphanage leavers attend. DRI concluded that the orphanage system serves as a recruitment tool for traffickers.

cases.title: Bosnia — trafficking of women and girls; IPTF monitors and SFOR/DynCorp contractors
cases.who: Traffickers and bar owners; local Bosnian police; UN International Police Task Force (IPTF) monitors; US SFOR civilian contractors (DynCorp)
cases.what: Human Rights Watch's November 2002 report 'Hopes Betrayed' documented women and girls trafficked mostly from Moldova, Romania and Ukraine into post-war Bosnia and held in debt bondage in bars and brothels. Local police were found acting as owners, guards and clients; 18 IPTF monitors who purchased women, visited brothels or faced trafficking-related charges went home, and none was confirmed prosecuted. A US Army CID report documented DynCorp contractors buying women from brothels; one confessed to buying a woman (with an Uzi) for 1,600 Deutschmarks. On 2 August 2002 a British employment tribunal unanimously found DynCorp had unfairly dismissed IPTF monitor Kathryn Bolkovac after she reported the trafficking.
cases.cover_up: Immunity: IPTF monitors were repatriated rather than prosecuted (18 returned home; HRW found no prosecution by Nov 2002); DynCorp contractors were sent home, preventing their use as witnesses; DynCorp fired whistleblower Kathryn Bolkovac in April 2001.

cases.title: Kosovo — trafficking for forced prostitution and the international presence (Amnesty 2004)
cases.who: Criminal networks; demand from NATO KFOR soldiers, UN police and international staff
cases.what: Amnesty International's May 2004 report said Kosovo had become a major destination for women and girls trafficked for forced prostitution since NATO troops and UN administrators arrived in 1999, with the international presence generating 80% of traffickers' income at the time. Women and girls were brought mainly from Moldova, Romania, Ukraine and Russia via Serbia, and local girls were also abducted. The UN peacekeeping department acknowledged in 2004 that peacekeepers had 'come to be seen as part of the problem in trafficking rather than the solution'.
cases.cover_up: Amnesty found no evidence of criminal proceedings against any military personnel in their home countries.

cases.title: Ukraine — wartime risk to evacuated institutional children; officials allegedly complicit (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Criminal networks; some institution officials
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says child sex trafficking in Ukraine is underreported and criminals are trying to build online networks to exploit Ukrainian children internationally; children evacuated from at least 195 facilities, including those with disabilities, are at high risk; and Ukrainian refugee women and children are vulnerable in Germany, France, Italy, Spain, Bulgaria and the UK. Ukraine convicted 24 traffickers in 2024, only six with prison terms.
cases.cover_up: Officials of several state-run residential institutions were allegedly complicit or negligent in trafficking of children in their care; no complicit officials convicted for the eighth year running.

networks.name: SS Race and Settlement Main Office (RuSHA) and Lebensborn e.V.
networks.what: RuSHA racially screened children in occupied territories and Lebensborn ran camps and homes from which selected children were placed with German families under new identities. The Nuremberg RuSHA trial (1947–48) ruled the kidnapping and Germanization of children part of genocide.

networks.name: Russian state system for transfer, adoption and 're-education' of Ukrainian children
networks.what: ICC arrest warrants (17 March 2023) for Vladimir Putin and Commissioner Maria Lvova-Belova for unlawful deportation and transfer of children. Yale HRL identified at least 43 camps in Russia and Crimea where at least 6,000 Ukrainian children were held in 2022. Ukraine counts 20,651 deported and/or forcibly displaced children and 2,752 returned (Oct 2026).

patterns.pattern: Peacekeepers and aid workers in crisis zones
patterns.role: Mission or crisis zone where children were abused
patterns.role_note: Kosovo — trafficking for forced prostitution and the international presence (Amnesty 2004).
patterns.pattern_summary: In war zones and refugee camps, children have been sexually abused by soldiers and aid workers sent to protect them or to provide food and shelter. In 2002 a report by the UN refugee agency and Save the Children described aid workers and peacekeepers in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone trading food and other aid for sex with children. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that Sri Lankan peacekeepers had abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007, and 114 soldiers were sent home; none was jailed in Sri Lanka. In the Central African Republic, children reported abuse by French soldiers and UN troops in 2014 and 2015; French judges closed the case against the French soldiers in 2018 without charges. An independent commission found 83 alleged perpetrators among people working on the World Health Organization's Ebola response in the Democratic Republic of the Congo between 2018 and 2020, 21 of them WHO staff, and victims as young as 13. The UN has published yearly counts of these allegations against peacekeepers since 2004.
